segments.name: Tomato
segments.note: one row down the middle, staked; the whole bed is then reachable without stepping on it

segments.name: Carrot
segments.note: four rows 6 in apart — the densest bed you will grow, and it works

segments.name: Lettuce
segments.note: three rows 9 in apart; cut the outer leaves and it keeps going

segments.name: Garlic
segments.note: four rows 6 in apart each way — 30 in beds are made for garlic

segments.name: Bush bean
segments.note: two rows 12 in apart down a 30 in bed

notes: Tall crops are placed at the north end of the block so they don't shade the beds beside them.

plantings.name: Asparagus
plantings.why: the crops that come up before you can work the ground
plantings.site: Needs a deep, well-drained, weed-free site prepared a year ahead; lime to 6.5-7.0 pH before planting. It is a permanent, once-planted bed occupying ground for 15-20 years, so it never rotates through the vegetable beds.
plantings.watch_for: asparagus beetle and spotted asparagus beetle chewing spear tips, Fusarium crown rot on wet low-pH soil, asparagus rust on damp ferns
plantings.source: UMaine Bulletin #2071 Growing Asparagus in Maine; Eliot Coleman, The New Organic Grower (3rd ed.), perennial crops chapter.

plantings.name: Rhubarb
plantings.why: the crops that come up before you can work the ground
plantings.site: Well-drained loam, full sun, generous spacing (3-4 ft) — a crown rewards space and forgives most soils. It occupies its corner for a decade or more and gets split every 4-5 years, so it never rotates through the annual beds.
plantings.year_one: A cool-climate crop that needs our cold winters to go dormant — no Maine chill problem at all. Best started as a divided crown with 1-2 eyes and at least a 2-in cross-section of storage root; seed gives variable plants. Do NOT harvest any stalks in year one; harvest from year two on, never more than half the stalks, and stop by about August 31 so the crown rebuilds for winter. Remove flower stalks as they form. Dig, split and replant the crown every four to five years to keep stalks thick. Leaves are oxalic-acid toxic; stalks only.
plantings.watch_for: crown rot in wet heavy soil, leaf fungal spots in cool damp weather, rhubarb curculio in weedy plantings
plantings.source: UMaine Bulletin #2514 Growing Rhubarb in Maine; Eliot Coleman, The New Organic Grower (3rd ed.), perennial crops chapter.

plantings.name: Strawberry
plantings.why: the fruit you pick standing up, mostly in year two and three
plantings.site: A short-lived perennial that must rotate: plant on new ground every 3-5 years to dodge soil-borne root rots. Full sun, sandy loam, 18-in matted rows. Not a permanent bed in the asparagus sense — it is a renewable perennial.
plantings.year_one: Technically perennial, practically a 3-5 year bed — plan to replant on fresh ground (never where tomatoes/peppers/eggplant grew: Verticillium). June-bearers: plant early spring, pinch ALL flowers the first year so runners fill an 18-in-apart matted row, mulch with 6-8 in of straw in mid-November and pull it off in spring. Earliglow, Wendy, Cavendish, Flavorfest and Jewel are the UMaine-tested performers. A fall/winter planting of day-neutrals (Seascape, Albion, Tribute, Tristar) can be grown as an annual for later fruit. Beds decline hard after year three — rotating through new ground is the honest plan.
plantings.watch_for: gray mold (Botrytis) in wet June weather, tarnished plant bug and strawberry bud weevil distorting fruit, red stele and Verticillium root rots — buy resistant varieties and move sites
plantings.source: UMaine Bulletin #2067 Growing Strawberries (site, spacing, varieties, renovation).

plantings.name: Highbush blueberry
plantings.why: the fruit you pick standing up, mostly in year two and three
plantings.site: Demands acid, well-drained sandy loam rich in organic matter — a dedicated ericaceous bed, kept separate from lime-loving vegetables. A 20-30 year permanent shrub planting, renewed by cane pruning, never rotated.
plantings.year_one: Soil is everything: highbush blueberry needs pH 4.5-5.2 and won't wait while you amend later — test and acidify with sulfur well before planting. Plant 2-3 year nursery bushes in early spring at 5-7 ft; two or more varieties improve set and spread the season (Patriot, Northland, Bluecrop, Blueray are UMaine's northern picks). Year-one and -two discipline: pick off all flower clusters both years, tolerate a small crop in year three, full crop at four to five. Prune dormant, January-March: canes older than six years come out. Protect below -25F is the real zone limit — Wiscasset coastal is fine.
plantings.watch_for: blueberry maggot in ripe fruit, mummy berry shriveling berries in wet springs, birds (netting is the only effective control)
plantings.source: UMaine Bulletin #2253 Growing Highbush Blueberries (pH, spacing, varieties, pruning, pests).

plantings.name: Apple
plantings.why: the long game — four to six years before the first real crop
plantings.site: Full sun, well-drained soil, at least 6 hours direct light; semi-dwarf at 15 ft spacing, dwarf at 6-8 ft. A permanent orchard tree producing for decades — entirely outside the vegetable rotation, with pollination, scab and deer management built in for the life of the tree.
plantings.year_one: The most winter-hardy tree fruit and the one Maine does best — most varieties are at home here; the coastal 5b/6a site is prime apple country. Plant bare-root in April/early May (fall planting is wrong for New England), graft union 2-3 in above ground, stake dwarf trees, never fertilize the planting hole. Train to central leader, head whips to 30-36 in. Most varieties need a second, compatible variety for pollination — plant two that bloom together. Scab is the disease that decides everything in a wet climate: choose resistant varieties (Liberty, Enterprise, Freedom, Pristine, CrimsonCrisp per UMaine) or spray from green tip. Dwarf on M.9/M.26 yields in year 3-4; be honest that standard trees take 6-8. Pick a mix that ripens from August into October.
plantings.watch_for: apple scab in our wet springs (plant resistant varieties), cedar-apple rust where junipers grow nearby, apple maggot and codling moth in the fruit, deer and voles on young trees
plantings.source: UMaine Cooperative Extension, Growing Fruit Trees in Maine: Types of Fruit Trees, Spacing Trees in an Orchard, Bulletin #2411 Planting and Early Care of Fruit Trees.

plantings.name: Pear (European)
plantings.why: the long game — four to six years before the first real crop
plantings.site: Full sun, well-drained soil; the largest of the hardy tree fruits, needing generous spacing (20 ft semi-dwarf, 30 ft standard). Slow to come into bearing (5-7 years) but very long-lived. Permanent orchard tree outside the rotation.
plantings.year_one: Pears are hardier than their reputation — the cold-hardy European varieties are rated for zone 4 and do fine in coastal Maine. The honest catches: they are the slowest of the tree fruits to bear (commonly 5-7 years even on dwarfing stock — plan for it), and fire blight decides the variety list: plant resistant types (Harrow Delight, Magness, Maxine, Potomac, Seckel per UMaine; Blake's Pride for market quality). They also grow large: give them the extra 5 ft beyond apple spacing. Two compatible varieties needed for pollination. Central-leader training, keep the crotch angles wide (45-60 deg) — narrow crotches split with a heavy crop. Asian pears are zone 5 but dislike Maine's winter temperature swings, so European types are the honest recommendation for Wiscasset.
plantings.watch_for: fire blight (the defining pear disease in the East — plant resistant varieties), pear psylla, codling moth; deer browse young trees
plantings.source: UMaine Cooperative Extension, Types of Fruit Trees (pear varieties and hardiness), Spacing Trees in an Orchard.

plantings.name: Hazelnut (American filbert)
plantings.why: the longest game, and the most reliable once it starts
plantings.site: American hazelnut: hardy zone 4, prefers well-drained soil but genuinely pH-adaptable, full sun for best nut set (light shade reduces yield). A multi-stemmed shrub 12-18 ft tall producing for 40-50 years. Needs a second plant for pollination; young plants must be caged from deer and voles for three years.
plantings.watch_for: eastern filbert blight (the disease that kills European hazels — American hazelnut is resistant), nut weevil leaving 'hit' marks on shells, squirrels/deer/voles/small rodents in the harvest
plantings.source: UMaine Home Garden News March 2022: American Hazelnut feature (hardiness, size, yields, harvest date, pests); Fedco Trees: American Hazelnut and Jefferson Hazelnut listings (spacing, culture).

alternatives.name: Jerusalem artichoke (sunchoke)
alternatives.why: Grows almost anywhere but prefers light sandy soil; full sun for best tuber bulk. It is a self-perpetuating, spreading perennial that never leaves the garden once planted — a deliberate permanent hedge, not a rotation crop.

alternatives.name: Sea kale
alternatives.why: A true perennial vegetable occupying permanent ground for a decade. Sharp-draining, sandy or chalky soil, full sun to part shade; thrives near coast. Never rotated — a permanent crown planting harvested for its forced spring shoots.

alternatives.name: Blackberry
alternatives.why: Perennial roots, biennial canes — each cane fruits once then dies, so it lives as a managed hedgerow with a trellis, outside the rotation. Full sun, well-drained sandy loam. Marginal hardiness in zone 5b: plant only in a sheltered, south-facing site.

alternatives.name: Lowbush blueberry (wild blueberry)
alternatives.why: Native to Maine's acid, sandy, well-drained coastal soils — replicate those conditions or it fails. A permanent ground-cover patch (1-2 ft tall) managed on a biennial mowing cycle, entirely outside the vegetable rotation.

alternatives.name: Elderberry
alternatives.why: Moist, fertile, well-drained soil, pH 5.5-6.5, full sun to part shade; tolerant of wetter ground than most berries. A suckering hedgerow shrub that must have room — not a bed crop. Renewed by cutting out canes older than three years.

alternatives.name: Honeyberry (haskap)
alternatives.why: Long-lived shrub (to 30 years), broadly pH-adaptable, needs moist well-drained soil and a second cultivar for pollination. Earliest-ripening berry in a Maine garden — a permanent planting that no annual bed can substitute for.

alternatives.name: Plum (hybrid/European)
alternatives.why: Full sun on a slope with air drainage — plums bloom early and the site is half the crop protection. Well-drained soil, pH 6.0-7.0, 12-18 ft spacing by rootstock. Permanent orchard tree; Japanese and European types must each be matched with their own kind for pollination.

alternatives.name: Sweet cherry
alternatives.why: MARGINAL in zone 5b: sweet cherries bloom earliest, suffer winter injury in cold years and need dwarf rootstock plus netting. Full sun, well-drained slope, 6-8 ft for dwarfs. Treat as an experiment here; a tart or duke cherry is the reliably productive choice.

alternatives.name: Tart (sour) cherry
alternatives.why: Full sun, well-drained soil, air-drained slope. The hardy, productive cherry for zone 5b — a naturally semidwarf permanent tree, self-fruitful, renewed by annual dormant pruning. Outside the vegetable rotation.

alternatives.name: Peach
alternatives.why: MARGINAL in zone 5b: UMaine puts lifetime expectancy at roughly 7 years in Maine, with winter bud kill below -10F the usual end. Needs full sun on an air-drained slope, pH 6.0-7.0. Plant the hardiest varieties and treat as a short-lived delight, not a long-term tree.

alternatives.name: Quince
alternatives.why: MARGINAL but viable in zone 5b coastal sites. Naturally dwarf tree needing less room; hardy to roughly -20F. Needs a long, warm fall to ripen fruit and has weak disease resistance (fire blight, quince rust). A specimen/preserve fruit tree, not a production staple.

roles.perennial-veg: the crops that come up before you can work the ground
roles.berry: the fruit you pick standing up, mostly in year two and three
roles.tree-fruit: the long game — four to six years before the first real crop
roles.nut: the longest game, and the most reliable once it starts

notes: red currant, black currant, gooseberry — Maine prohibits growing these in the counties with white pine blister rust, and a zip can't tell us your county. Left out on purpose.
Possible but a gamble this far north: blackberry, elderberry, sweet cherry, peach, quince. Hardiest varieties only, and the most sheltered spot you have.
permanent_plantings.year_one_rule: Nothing fruits in year one. Strip the flowers and the first fruit off, and put that year into roots and canes instead — it is the difference between a plant that crops for fifteen years and one that limps for five.

phases.title: Build the beds
phases.why: Everything in this plan assumes ground that is ready to take roots.

steps.text: Mark it out before you dig anything: 30 in beds, 30-inch beds with 12-inch paths between them. Worked from the path, never stood on. Narrow enough to reach the middle from either side, which is the whole point — compaction is what costs you yield.

Cheapest and quickest — sheet mulch. Flat cardboard, overlapped generously and soaked, then an inch of compost, then whatever mulch the town or the woods will give you. Plant straight into holes cut in it this season; the bed improves underneath you while you use it.

If what you have is lawn or hard-packed ground — and only then — one pass with a broadfork, or a single pass of a tiller, to break the pan. Sheet mulch over a hard lawn is a two-year proposition, and most people quit before the payoff. Tilling once to open ground up is a tool. Tilling it every year is what ruins it.
If you want to build the bed out of what is already on the property, this is the hugelkultur version, bottom to top:
sub: Cardboard flat on the ground, overlapped, soaked.
Woody material — branches, rotten logs, sticks, brush — filling the BOTTOM THIRD only. Thickest pieces lowest, gaps packed with smaller stuff. Water each layer as you go.
A sprinkle of native soil or old compost over the wood, as inoculum.
Leaves, straw, grass clippings, garden waste.
Topsoil or a compost-mix to fill the last few inches.

steps.text: Two honest caveats on hugelkultur: it sinks as the wood rots, so put anything perennial at the edges and not in the middle; and fresh wood ties up nitrogen for a season, so give the heavy feeders a mid-season top-dress. Do not sow carrots or anything with fine seed into a fresh one — it will not be an even seedbed yet.

phases.title: Feed the soil, not the plant
phases.when: the same weekend as the beds
phases.why: Fertility you build is fertility you don't buy again next year.

steps.text: Compost on top, 1–2 inches, once in spring. Do not dig it in — the worms and the frost will take it down for you.

Coleman's fertility trick is a rotation, not a bag: at Four Season Farm roughly half the ground is in deep-rooted green manure at any time — clover, vetch, field peas — grown to be cut down and left on the surface. It feeds the soil, smothers weeds and takes the place of bought nitrogen.
Free amendments worth having here: seaweed and leaf mould. Rinse the seaweed if it is fresh, and stockpile leaves in a wire ring — two years later they are the best mulch you own.
Heavy feeders in this plan — tomato — get a mid-season top-dress of compost at flowering. That single handful is most of the difference between a crop and a glut.

phases.title: Layout and spacing
phases.why: The counts below are what fits at proper spacing. Crowding is the mistake that costs the most yield for the least regret.

steps.text: Bed geometry: 30-inch beds, 12-inch paths (Coleman's system). Worked from the path, never stood on. Narrow enough to reach the middle from either side, which is the whole point — compaction is what costs you yield.
Bed 1: 1. Tomato 2 plants in 5 ft (tall — north end) · then 2. Carrot 48 plants in 3 ft · then 3. Lettuce 12 plants in 4 ft.
Bed 2: 4. Garlic 48 plants in 6 ft · then 5. Bush bean 36 plants in 6 ft.
The numbered badges on the drawing match these numbers, one crop run each.
Families in this plan: Allium, Solanaceae, Apiaceae, Fabaceae, Asteraceae — all different, which is what you want. Next year, keep each family moving to a different bed.
And tell the plan what was in each bed last year — that is the one input a rotation cannot invent, and it is worth more than any fertiliser.

phases.title: Planting and succession
phases.why: A bed should always be doing something, and it should never all arrive at once.

steps.text: Tomato: start inside the week of Mar 9 — 7 weeks before your Apr 27 frost — and set them out after it. Transplant-first is the discipline here: it buys weeks and it beats the weeds.
Lettuce: start inside the week of Mar 30 — 4 weeks before your Apr 27 frost — and set them out after it. Transplant-first is the discipline here: it buys weeks and it beats the weeds.
Sown straight into the bed, once the ground is workable: garlic, carrot, bush bean.

Succession — this is the one that decides whether you eat well all summer or drown in one week: carrot every 21 days, bush bean every 14 days, lettuce every 14 days. Sow a short row, not a long one, and keep it up until late July.
No obvious gap in the season as planted — the succession sowings above are what keeps it that way.

phases.title: Pests and beneficials — the short version that works
phases.why: Most companion-planting advice is folklore. These four things have evidence behind them; the rest of the chart does not.

steps.text: Insectary strip. Sow sweet alyssum — or dill, cilantro, phacelia — along one path edge and let it flower. In field trials roughly 10% of the area in alyssum was enough to hold aphids down, by feeding hoverflies and tiny parasitic wasps that eat them. This is the highest-value square foot in most gardens.

Row cover as a barrier. Over cucumbers and anything brassica from planting until they flower — it beats every spray because the pest never lands. You must lift it for pollination, and you must not leave it on in a heatwave.

On marigolds, since they come up every year: French and African marigolds do suppress root-knot nematodes — but only as a solid crop grown for a couple of months and then tilled in, not as a plant set beside the tomatoes. In Maine the nematodes are rarely the problem anyway, so grow them for the hoverflies and the colour, not for the myth.

Scout twice a week, and know what you're looking for: Garlic — white rot — never replant garlic, onion or leek where alliums grew; leek moth; Tomato — late blight in a wet August, hornworms, blossom end rot from uneven watering rather than disease; Carrot — carrot rust fly, forked or split roots from fresh manure, stones, or drying out; Bush bean — Mexican bean beetle, bean rust in a wet year, rabbits while the plants are small; Lettuce — slugs (the real enemy here), bolting in heat, bottom rot in a wet spell. Twice a week with a coffee beats any spray, because you catch it while it's still squashable.

Alternate an early crop and a late crop in the same bed — extension guidance, and Coleman's whole spring-to-fall sequence runs on it. Soil that is never bare does not grow weeds, and cover is the cheapest pest control there is.

phases.title: Water
phases.why: Deep and infrequent beats a daily sprinkle — it drives roots down instead of teaching them to stay shallow.

steps.text: One soaker line down the middle of each 30 in bed, under the mulch. Ten minutes of drip twice a week does more than an hour with a hose.
Water at the base in the morning. Wet leaves at night is how you grow blight instead of tomatoes.
Mulch 2–3 inches: straw, leaves, grass clippings. It halves the watering and it is where the slugs live — so keep it back an inch from the stems.
Garlic: Water through spring; stop three weeks before harvest.
Tomato: Deep soak twice a week; keep leaves dry to slow blight.
Carrot: Shallow, frequent water until established, then deep weekly.

phases.title: Stretch the season
phases.when: late August, and again in October
phases.why: This is Coleman's actual specialty, and it is why zone 5 does not have to mean six months off.

steps.text: A cold frame at one end of a bed, hinged on the south side, glazed with the storm window already in your basement. Open it on sunny days or you will cook what you are protecting.
Quick hoops — bent wire or conduit over a bed, with row cover or clear plastic clipped on. Cheapest protected growing there is, and it moves to next year's bed in ten minutes.
Standing into the cold, from this plan: garlic, carrot, lettuce. Sow the greens in late summer, not spring — they come through the winter and they are the first thing you eat in March.
Leave carrots in the ground under a foot of mulch and dig them as you need them, all winter. They get sweeter for it.

phases.title: Harvest, and the week it all lands
phases.why: Because the peak is the part that decides whether you eat well or compost it.

steps.text: Everything in the main season lands between Jun 2 and Aug 3. That peak is the week that breaks people.
Pick every second day once the glut starts, and pick into the house, not into a bucket on the porch. A day on the porch is a day off the shelf life.
The glut itself is what The Preservation Run is for — what to can, freeze, cellar and ferment, in the order the harvest arrives.

phases.title: The permanent plantings
phases.when: any time in the first year
phases.why: A fifth of this list isn't a season crop. These take a position for fifteen years, so they are chosen once and planted properly or regretted for a decade.

steps.text: Nothing fruits in year one. Strip the flowers and the first fruit off, and put that year into roots and canes instead — it is the difference between a plant that crops for fifteen years and one that limps for five.

These 7 don't rotate and don't take a bed: Asparagus, Rhubarb, Strawberry, Highbush blueberry, Apple, Pear (European), Hazelnut (American filbert). Give them their own ground — a border, a cane row, a sod patch, an orchard corner — and they will still be cropping when the beds have been rebuilt twice.

Asparagus: 1 ft apart, 3 years to the first real crop, about 15 years of life. Needs a deep, well-drained, weed-free site prepared a year ahead; lime to 6.5-7.0 pH before planting. It is a permanent, once-planted bed occupying ground for 15-20 years, so it never rotates through the vegetable beds. Watch for asparagus beetle and spotted asparagus beetle chewing spear tips.

Rhubarb: 3.5 ft apart, 2 years to the first real crop, about 10 years of life. Well-drained loam, full sun, generous spacing (3-4 ft) — a crown rewards space and forgives most soils. It occupies its corner for a decade or more and gets split every 4-5 years, so it never rotates through the annual beds. Watch for crown rot in wet heavy soil.

Strawberry: 1.5 ft apart, 2 years to the first real crop, about 4 years of life. A short-lived perennial that must rotate: plant on new ground every 3-5 years to dodge soil-borne root rots. Full sun, sandy loam, 18-in matted rows. Not a permanent bed in the asparagus sense — it is a renewable perennial. Watch for gray mold (Botrytis) in wet June weather.

Highbush blueberry: 6 ft apart, 4 years to the first real crop, about 25 years of life. Demands acid, well-drained sandy loam rich in organic matter — a dedicated ericaceous bed, kept separate from lime-loving vegetables. A 20-30 year permanent shrub planting, renewed by cane pruning, never rotated. Watch for blueberry maggot in ripe fruit.

Apple: 15 ft apart, 5 years to the first real crop, about 35 years of life. Full sun, well-drained soil, at least 6 hours direct light; semi-dwarf at 15 ft spacing, dwarf at 6-8 ft. A permanent orchard tree producing for decades — entirely outside the vegetable rotation, with pollination, scab and deer management built in for the life of the tree. Watch for apple scab in our wet springs (plant resistant varieties).

Pear (European): 20 ft apart, 6 years to the first real crop, about 40 years of life. Full sun, well-drained soil; the largest of the hardy tree fruits, needing generous spacing (20 ft semi-dwarf, 30 ft standard). Slow to come into bearing (5-7 years) but very long-lived. Permanent orchard tree outside the rotation. Watch for fire blight (the defining pear disease in the East — plant resistant varieties).

Hazelnut (American filbert): 12 ft apart, 4 years to the first real crop, about 40 years of life. American hazelnut: hardy zone 4, prefers well-drained soil but genuinely pH-adaptable, full sun for best nut set (light shade reduces yield). A multi-stemmed shrub 12-18 ft tall producing for 40-50 years. Needs a second plant for pollination; young plants must be caged from deer and voles for three years. Watch for eastern filbert blight (the disease that kills European hazels — American hazelnut is resistant).
red currant, black currant, gooseberry — Maine prohibits growing these in the counties with white pine blister rust, and a zip can't tell us your county. Left out on purpose.
Possible but a gamble this far north: blackberry, elderberry, sweet cherry, peach, quince. Hardiest varieties only, and the most sheltered spot you have.

geometry_dims.label: 30-inch beds, 12-inch paths (Coleman's system)
geometry_dims.why: Worked from the path, never stood on. Narrow enough to reach the middle from either side, which is the whole point — compaction is what costs you yield.
